# Two Different Jobs

Git uses cryptographic keys for two jobs that are easy to confuse. Almost every
confusing error message comes from mixing them up.

**Authentication** proves to GitHub that you are allowed to push. It happens at
the network boundary, once per push. *Everyone needs this.*

**Signing** stamps each commit so others can verify who wrote it. It happens on
your own machine, at commit time, and the stamp is permanent. *Most people never
need this.*

Sections 2 and 3 cover authentication and are all that is required for this
course. Sections 4 and 5 cover signing and are optional.

::: {.callout-note}
Both jobs use **public-key cryptography**: a *private key* that stays on your
machine and a *public key* you hand out freely. Anything the private key signs,
the public key can verify — and the math does not run backwards, so the public
key reveals nothing about the private one.
:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Start Here: HTTPS (No Keys Required)

This is the recommended setup. It works identically on macOS, Windows, and
Linux, requires no key generation, and has the fewest ways to fail.

## Tell Git who you are

The email **must match** an email registered on your GitHub account, or your
commits will not be linked to your profile.

```r
install.packages(c("usethis", "gitcreds"))

usethis::use_git_config(
  user.name  = "Your Name",
  user.email = "you@usu.edu"
)
```

## Create a Personal Access Token

A Personal Access Token (PAT) is a long password that GitHub generates for you.
This command opens GitHub in your browser with the correct permissions already
checked.

```r
usethis::create_github_token()
```

Before clicking **Generate token**, set the expiration to **90 days** or longer.
The default is 30 days, which will expire in the middle of the semester.

Copy the token immediately. GitHub will never show it to you again.

## Store the token

```r
gitcreds::gitcreds_set()
```

Paste the token when prompted. It is saved in the macOS Keychain or Windows
Credential Manager, so you only do this once.

## Confirm everything works

```r
usethis::git_sitrep()
```

This prints a full report on your Git and GitHub configuration. If something is
wrong, the output will say what. **Run this first whenever you are stuck, and
show the output when you ask for help.**

::: {.callout-important}
## Turn signing off before you start

If you have used GitHub Desktop before, or copied a config from a blog post,
commit signing may already be enabled — and it will fail inside Positron in
confusing ways. Run this once, even if you think you do not need it:

```bash
git config --global commit.gpgsign false
```
:::

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Optional: SSH for Authentication

SSH keys are an alternative to a PAT. They never expire, but they add a key
generation step and can be blocked on networks that close port 22. Use HTTPS
unless you have a reason not to.

## Generate a key

```bash
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "you@usu.edu"
```

Press Enter to accept the default location (`~/.ssh/id_ed25519`). A passphrase is
optional but recommended.

## Add the public key to GitHub

```bash
cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
```

Copy the output. On GitHub, go to **Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New SSH key**,
choose key type **Authentication key**, and paste.

## Test it

```bash
ssh -T git@github.com
```

Success looks like: `Hi username! You've successfully authenticated...`

# Optional: SSH for Signing

If you want signed commits, **use SSH rather than GPG**. It produces the same
"Verified" badge on GitHub with far fewer moving parts — no background agent, no
passphrase dialogs, no expiration dates.

```bash
git config --global gpg.format ssh
git config --global user.signingkey ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub
git config --global commit.gpgsign true
```

Then add the **same public key to GitHub a second time**, this time with key type
**Signing key**. GitHub treats authentication and signing as separate
registrations even for identical keys.

Verify:

```bash
git commit --allow-empty -m "signing test"
git log --show-signature -1
```

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Optional: GPG for Signing

GPG is the older, more capable, and considerably more fragile option. Use it only
if a project you contribute to requires OpenPGP signatures specifically.

## Install and generate

```bash
brew install gnupg          # macOS
gpg --full-generate-key     # choose ECC (Curve25519), or RSA 4096
```

## Find your key ID

```bash
gpg --list-secret-keys --keyid-format=long
```

Look for the line beginning `sec`. The key ID is the part after the slash:

```
sec   ed25519/A507164A8478CED8 2026-09-19 [SC]
                ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
```

Check two things in this output. The key must not be marked `[expired]` or
`[revoked]`, and it must carry the `S` capability — a key marked only `[E]` can
encrypt but cannot sign.

## Configure Git

```bash
git config --global user.signingkey A507164A8478CED8
git config --global commit.gpgsign true
git config --global --unset gpg.format   # clear any leftover SSH setting
```

## Add the public key to GitHub

```bash
gpg --armor --export A507164A8478CED8
```

Copy the entire block, including the `-----BEGIN-----` and `-----END-----` lines.
On GitHub: **Settings → SSH and GPG keys → New GPG key**.

## Required on macOS: a graphical passphrase prompt

GPG's default passphrase prompt needs a terminal to draw in. Positron does not
provide one, so signing fails there even when it works in the shell. Install a
GUI prompt instead:

```bash
brew install pinentry-mac
echo "pinentry-program $(brew --prefix)/bin/pinentry-mac" >> ~/.gnupg/gpg-agent.conf
gpgconf --kill gpg-agent
```

Also add this line to `~/.zshrc`, which fixes the same error in the terminal:

```bash
export GPG_TTY=$(tty)
```

Test from a terminal before returning to Positron:

```bash
echo test | gpg --clearsign
```

If a passphrase dialog appears and a signed block is printed, you are set.
Restart Positron so it picks up the new agent.

{{< pagebreak >}}

# Why Positron Specifically Causes Trouble

Two failure modes are specific to running Git inside a graphical IDE. Both
produce errors that look like Git problems but are not.

**The IDE does not see your shell PATH.** Positron launched from the Dock or
Start Menu never reads `~/.zshrc`, so tools installed by Homebrew can be
invisible to it. A command that works perfectly in the terminal fails inside the
IDE. The fix is to give Git an absolute path:

```bash
git config --global gpg.program /opt/homebrew/bin/gpg
```

**The IDE has no terminal for prompts.** Anything that needs to ask you a
question interactively — a GPG passphrase, most commonly — has nowhere to draw
it. This is what `pinentry-mac` solves.

Both are reasons to prefer HTTPS authentication and no signing while you are
learning Git.

# Troubleshooting

| Error message | Cause | Fix |
|---------------------|-------------------|-----------------------------|
| `cannot run gpg: No such file or directory` | Positron cannot see `gpg` on its PATH | Set `gpg.program` to the absolute path, or turn signing off |
| `gpg: skipped "...": No secret key` | No private key matches your `user.email` | Set `user.signingkey` explicitly, or check for an expired key |
| `Couldn't load public key <fingerprint>` | `gpg.format` is `ssh` but `user.signingkey` is a GPG key ID | Pick one format; in SSH mode the value must be a path to a `.pub` file |
| `signing failed: Inappropriate ioctl for device` | Passphrase prompt has no terminal | Install `pinentry-mac`; set `GPG_TTY` in `~/.zshrc` |
| `Authentication failed` on push | PAT expired or was never stored | Re-run `usethis::create_github_token()` then `gitcreds::gitcreds_set()` |
| `Permission denied (publickey)` | SSH key not registered with GitHub | Add `~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub` under **Authentication key** |

: Common Git errors and what they actually mean {tbl-colwidths="[34,26,40]"}

# Starting Over

If your configuration has become tangled, inspect all of it at once:

```bash
git config --global --list
```

To clear the signing-related settings and return to a clean state:

```bash
git config --global --unset commit.gpgsign
git config --global --unset gpg.format
git config --global --unset gpg.program
git config --global --unset user.signingkey
```

Your authentication setup is separate and is not affected by these commands.

# Further Reading

*Happy Git and GitHub for the useR* by Jenny Bryan is the standard reference for
this material in the R ecosystem, and it is free online at
<https://happygitwithr.com>. Chapters 9 through 11 cover authentication in more
detail than this handout.
